title: Manhattan Park construction ramped up sharply in FY2025
plain_english_explanation: The Parks Millage capital project for Manhattan Park (fund 408, dept 788) spent $2,377,027 in FY2025, up from $638,849 in FY2024 (+272%, +$1,738,178). This is the construction phase of a voter-approved parks millage project: FY2024 journal entries show design work (Viridis Design Group $121,080) and early site work (Groundhawg Excavating $489,983), while FY2025 entries show the general contractor Katerberg-VerHage Inc billing $1,939,970 against 408-788-9700.00, matching check-register payments to Katerberg-VerHage of $1,981,311 in FY2025. This is planned capital-project spending, not an overrun.
source: GL Transactions 7.1.24-6.30.25.xlsx (ActivitybyGLJournal); FY2025 Check Regsiter.xlsx (file labeled FY2025, checks dated FY2025)

title: Parks playground capital projects wound down after FY2024
plain_english_explanation: Parks playground projects (fund 408, dept 785) spent $3,290,943 in FY2024 but only $125,806 in FY2025 (-96%, -$3,165,137). FY2024 included $2,519,302 of capital expenditures plus $699,073 of equipment. This pattern is consistent with a completed project phase; the offsetting increase is the Manhattan Park construction above. No concern indicated.
source: GL Activity by Journal Type 7.1.23-6.30.24.xlsx; GL Transactions 7.1.24-6.30.25.xlsx

title: City buildings capital spending rose 156%, driven by salt-barn build and HVAC replacements
plain_english_explanation: City buildings capital expenditures (101-265-9700.00) rose from $329,155 in FY2024 to $843,495 in FY2025 (+$514,340). Journal descriptions identify the pieces: a DPW salt/aggregate storage building (Clear Heights Construction LLC ~$275,410 across deposit/progress/final payments, plus ANS Steel Buildings $33,690 and related site work), HVAC capital replacements (Northwest Kent Mechanical ~$110,077, Seaman’s Mechanical ~$105,741), CIP flooring (Seelye Group $109,118), and an EGR library study room (Custer Workplace Interiors $56,285). These are one-time capital projects.

title: Employee pharmacy costs jumped 153% in the health care fund
plain_english_explanation: Pharmacy claims in the employee Health Care Fund (677-852-8330.00) rose from $161,771 in FY2024 to $409,879 in FY2025 (+$248,108, +153%). Journal entries show routine twice-monthly Blue Cross Blue Shield claim payments with no single anomalous payment; the increase is spread across the year, suggesting higher claim volume or drug costs rather than one event. Medical (HRA) claims also rose $661,052 to $841,967 (+27%). Total Health Care Fund spending rose 31% ($1.54M to $2.03M). The underlying cause (utilization, specialty drugs, enrollment changes) cannot be determined from these files.

title: OPEB (retiree health) trust medical claims tripled
plain_english_explanation: The Other Post-Employment Benefits trust fund (736) spent $432,368 in FY2025 vs $255,699 in FY2024 (+69%, +$176,669), driven by medical claims (736-560-8340.00) rising from $59,967 to $187,942 (+$127,975). The files show only routine BCBS claim entries; the reason for higher retiree medical utilization is not determinable from these files.

title: FY2026 fleet purchases are over budget at the 75% mark
plain_english_explanation: Motor Equipment vehicle purchases (692-570-9700.21) have an amended FY2026 budget of $1,180,000 with $1,441,260 spent through 3/31/2026 (122% of budget, $261,260 over). Transaction detail shows a planned fleet-replacement cycle: a $567,091 International sewer truck (Fredrickson Supply), a $118,888 loader and $77,662 excavator (Michigan Cat), two dump trucks ~$114,861 each plus upfits (West Michigan International / Truck & Trailer Specialties), and $121,166 for two truck replacements (Gorno Ford). IMPORTANT TIMING CAVEAT: this is a 3/31 snapshot; capital budgets are routinely amended, and fleet purchases are lumpy by nature. Whether the budget will be amended to cover this cannot be determined from these files.

title: AJZ Concrete payments spiked in spring 2026
plain_english_explanation: Payments to AJZ Concrete LLC were $61,869 across Jul-May of FY2025 vs $360,208 across Jul-May of FY2026 (+482%), with the jump concentrated in April-May 2026 (including a $109,355 payment on 5/28/2026 and $59,299 on 4/22/2026). In FY2025, AJZ work was charged to street routine-maintenance contractual services (202/203-463-8010.00). The spring-2026 payments postdate the 3/31/2026 YTD file, so their project coding is not visible in these files; the pattern is consistent with seasonal concrete/sidewalk work, but the specific project cannot be verified from these files.
source: FY2024 Check Register.xlsx / FY2025 Check Regsiter.xlsx (check-date fiscal years FY2025/FY2026)

title: Sidewalk repair program spending tripled
plain_english_explanation: Sidewalk spending (204-444) rose from $193,073 in FY2024 to $432,331 in FY2025 (+124%, +$239,258), all in the sidewalk repair program account (204-444-9350.04: $143,170 to $432,331). This looks like an expanded repair program year; the FY2026 picture is not yet visible in the YTD file at the account level checked.
source: GL Activity by Journal Type 7.1.23-6.30.24.xlsx; GL Transactions 7.1.24-6.30.25.xlsx

title: Storm sewer spending fell 74% year over year
plain_english_explanation: Storm sewer spending (204-445) fell from $461,625 in FY2024 to $119,819 in FY2025 (-$341,806, -74%). Capital project spending is lumpy by nature; without project schedules these files cannot show whether this is timing or a reduced program.
source: GL Activity by Journal Type 7.1.23-6.30.24.xlsx; GL Transactions 7.1.24-6.30.25.xlsx

title: Pension contribution (general administration) decreased $280,000
plain_english_explanation: The defined-benefit pension contribution booked in General Administration (101-875-7190.01) fell from $1,380,000 in FY2024 to $1,100,000 in FY2025 (-20%, -$280,000), driving most of the $310,273 decrease in the 101-875 department. Contribution amounts are typically set by actuarial valuation; the reason for the decrease is not in these files.
source: GL Activity by Journal Type 7.1.23-6.30.24.xlsx; GL Transactions 7.1.24-6.30.25.xlsx

title: Professional and contractual services totaled $2.34M in FY2025
plain_english_explanation: Accounts for contractual/professional services (8010-series plus 7080/8180 legal) totaled $2,338,701 in FY2025 vs $2,202,763 in FY2024 (+6%). Largest pieces: city-attorney contractual wages $250,944 (101-210-7080.00; journal entries attribute ~$191,439 to Varnum LLP legal services), engineering contractual $203,071 (101-447-8010.00; ~$203K attributed to Hubbell Roth Clark), finance contractual $140,179, public safety contractual $126,630, and street routine-maintenance contractual $227,312 across funds 202/203. This is a normal operating cost, flagged only for its size.

title: Vendor concentration: top 10 vendors are 60% of check payments
plain_english_explanation: Excluding property-tax pass-throughs, the top 10 vendors by FY2025 check payments account for 59.8% of city-vendor check dollars (top 5: 42.1%, top 20: 71.9%). The top of the list is dominated by a few large, explainable items: wholesale water purchases from the Grand Rapids City Treasurer ($2.05M), Manhattan Park contractor Katerberg-VerHage ($1.98M), road contractor Michigan Paving ($1.84M), the Kent District Library contract/millage ($1.05M), and bond debt service via US Bank ($974K). Concentration reflects capital-project lumpiness, not a control issue.

title: Purchasing-card payments ($545K) lack transaction detail in these files
plain_english_explanation: Monthly payments to Fifth Third Bank totaling $545,138 in FY2025 (12 payments, e.g., $99,046 on 5/31/2025) are consistent with a city purchasing-card program, but the check register shows only the monthly settlement amounts, not the underlying purchases. Nothing here suggests a problem; the detail simply is not in the files provided.

title: Duplicate-looking payments found are recurring monthly services, not errors
plain_english_explanation: A scan for same-vendor, same-amount payments within 31 days of each other (>= $1,000) found 32 instances, all consistent with recurring services: monthly janitorial service (JO Cleaning Service, $12,312/month), monthly IT service (I3 Business Solutions, ~$1,555/month), and repeat small-quantity material orders (Cannonsburg Wood Products). No unexplained duplicates were found.

title: Michigan Paving payments down 52% in the like-for-like window
plain_english_explanation: Payments to Michigan Paving & Materials Co. were $1,078,905 in Jul-May FY2025 vs $519,593 in Jul-May FY2026 (-52%). GL attribution shows FY2025 payments charged to local/major street construction (203-451-9730.00: $1,217,821; 202-451-9730.00: $140,162). Road construction is seasonal and project-driven; whether FY2026 work is deferred to summer months or reduced cannot be determined from these files (the YTD file ends 3/31/2026, before paving season).
source: FY2024 Check Register.xlsx / FY2025 Check Regsiter.xlsx

title: 51 accounts over budget at the 75% mark of FY2026 (timing caveat applies)
plain_english_explanation: At 3/31/2026 (75% through FY2026), 51 expenditure accounts show year-to-date spending above their full-year amended budget. Most are small-dollar; the largest is fleet vehicle purchases (692-570-9700.21, $261,260 over — see separate flag). Others over by >$10K include public-safety uniforms (101-345-7400.01, +$18,253), motor-equipment repairs (692-570-9300.00, +$14,730), winter-maintenance wages (203-478-7060.00, +$14,372), OPEB pharmacy (736-560-8330.00, +$12,924), and motor-equipment parts (692-570-7540.00, +$12,463). IMPORTANT: budget-vs-actual at an interim date is NOT an overrun finding — many accounts spend seasonally (winter maintenance, road salt), some reflect one-time purchases, and budgets are routinely amended before year-end. Only year-end actuals vs final amended budgets determine true overruns.
